title: The airway plan and the nose
summary: Upper and lower tracts, conducting and respiratory zones, and the nose that conditions every breath.
objectives: Divide the respiratory tract into upper and lower parts and into conducting and respiratory zones
Name the parts of the nasal septum and the bones of the nasal roof and floor
Explain how the conchae, mucosa and venous plexus warm, moisten and filter air
takeaways: Upper tract: nose, nasal cavity, pharynx. Lower tract: larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs.
Septum = perpendicular plate of ethmoid + vomer + septal cartilage.
Conchae make airflow turbulent; mucus, cilia and warm blood condition the air.
Roof = cribriform plate; floor = hard palate; the choanae open into the nasopharynx.

steps.title: Two tracts, two zones
steps.text:
The upper respiratory tract is the nose, nasal cavity and pharynx; the lower respiratory tract is the larynx, trachea, bronchi and lungs.

A second split is by job. The conducting zone (nose down to the terminal bronchioles) only moves air and conditions it: warming, moistening and filtering. The respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli) is where gas exchange happens.

check.q: Where does the conducting zone end?
check.a: At the terminal bronchioles; everything beyond them belongs to the respiratory zone.

steps.title: Nostrils, vestibule and septum
steps.text:
Air enters through the external nares (nostrils), whose shape is set by the nasal cartilages, chiefly the major alar cartilage. Just inside is the nasal vestibule, lined by skin-like stratified squamous epithelium with coarse guard hairs that stop large particles.

The nasal septum divides the cavity in two. It has three parts: the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above, the vomer below and the septal cartilage in front.

check.q: Which three parts build the nasal septum?
check.a: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, the vomer and the septal cartilage.

steps.title: Conchae, meatuses and mucosa
steps.text:
Three shelves project from each lateral wall: the superior, middle and inferior nasal conchae, each roofing a groove called a meatus. They make the airstream turbulent, so every parcel of air touches the lining.

That lining is a mucous membrane of respiratory epithelium: pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells with goblet cells. Sticky mucus traps dust and moistens the air, and a superficial venous plexus in the connective tissue beneath warms it.

check.q: What epithelium lines the nasal cavity proper, and what does the vestibule have instead?
check.a: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells; the vestibule has stratified squamous epithelium.

steps.title: Roof, floor and the back door
steps.text:
The roof of the nasal cavity is mostly the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, with the frontal, nasal and sphenoid bones at its slopes. The floor is the hard palate: the palatine processes of the maxillae in front and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind.

At the back the internal nares (choanae) open into the nasopharynx. The paranasal sinuses and the shape of the oral cavity add sonority (resonance) to the voice.

check.q: Which two bony parts make the hard palate?
check.a: The palatine processes of the maxillae and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones.

practice.q: Which organ belongs to the LOWER respiratory tract?
practice.why: The lower tract starts at the larynx; the pharynx and nose are upper tract.

practice.q: Put the path of inhaled air in order
items: Nasal cavity and meatuses beneath the conchae

practice.q: What is the main job of the nasal conchae?
choices: Make airflow turbulent so air meets the mucosa
practice.why: Turbulence brings air into contact with the warm, wet, sticky lining.

practice.q: Name the three things the conducting zone does to inspired air.
practice.a: Warms it, moistens it and filters it.

practice.q: What warms the air in the nasal cavity, and what traps the dust?
practice.a: A superficial venous plexus under the mucosa warms it; mucus from goblet cells traps dust.

practice.q: Which structures form the roof and which the floor of the nasal cavity?
practice.a: Roof: cribriform plate of the ethmoid (with the frontal, nasal and sphenoid bones). Floor: hard palate = palatine processes of maxillae + horizontal plates of palatine bones.

practice.q: What stops large particles at the nostril?
practice.why: Coarse hairs in the skin-lined vestibule act as the first filter.

practice.q: Name the upper respiratory tract organs.
practice.a: Nose, nasal cavity and pharynx.

practice.q: Besides the paranasal sinuses, what shapes the sonority (resonance) of the voice?
practice.a: The shape of the oral cavity, altered by the tongue and lips.

practice.q: In a midsagittal section, which tooth marks the front end of the hard palate?
practice.a: The central (medial) incisor.

title: Pharynx and larynx
summary: Three levels of throat, nine cartilages of voice box, and the folds that make a voice.
objectives: Name the three parts of the pharynx and what passes through each
Identify the laryngeal cartilages, their cartilage type and the connecting membranes
Distinguish vestibular from vocal folds and explain how pitch is changed
Compare the cat larynx with the human one
takeaways: Nasopharynx (air only) → oropharynx (air and food) → laryngopharynx (into oesophagus).
Thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform: hyaline. Epiglottis: elastic.
Vocal folds + the gap between them = glottis; tighter folds give a higher pitch.
The larynx lies at C4–C6; its prominence is bigger in males because of testosterone.

steps.title: Three levels of pharynx
steps.text:
The nasopharynx sits behind the nasal cavity and carries air only; the openings of the auditory tubes are in its side walls. The oropharynx, behind the mouth, is a shared passage for food, liquid and air. The laryngopharynx lies above and behind the larynx and continues into the oesophagus.

During swallowing the soft palate and uvula rise to seal off the nasopharynx so food does not go up the nose.

check.q: Which part of the pharynx carries air only?
check.a: The nasopharynx.

steps.title: The laryngeal cartilages
steps.text:
The larynx (voice box) lies at about C4–C6. The thyroid cartilage is the largest: a shield of hyaline cartilage with a superior thyroid notch and a laryngeal prominence that grows larger in males under testosterone.

Below it the cricoid cartilage is a complete ring, narrow in front and broad behind. On the cricoid sit the paired arytenoid cartilages, which anchor the back ends of the vocal folds, capped by the small corniculate cartilages; the cuneiform cartilages lie in the fold in front of them.

check.q: Which laryngeal cartilage is a complete ring, and what shape is it?
check.a: The cricoid: narrow anteriorly and broad posteriorly, like a signet ring.

steps.title: Epiglottis and the membranes
steps.text:
The epiglottis is a leaf of elastic cartilage, so it bends and springs back. During swallowing the larynx rises and the epiglottis tips over the laryngeal inlet. Anything that still gets in triggers the cough reflex.

Sheets tie the cartilages together: the thyrohyoid membrane hangs the larynx from the hyoid bone, the quadrangular membrane runs from epiglottis to arytenoids, and the cricothyroid ligament joins cricoid to thyroid. A pad of pre-epiglottic fat (adipose tissue) sits in front of the epiglottis.

check.q: Why is the epiglottis made of elastic rather than hyaline cartilage?
check.a: It must bend repeatedly over the laryngeal inlet and spring back.

steps.title: Folds, glottis and pitch
steps.text:
Inside the larynx two pairs of folds project from the walls. The upper pair are the vestibular folds (false vocal cords); the lower pair are the vocal folds (true vocal cords), which vibrate to make sound. The vocal folds plus the opening between them form the glottis.

The intrinsic laryngeal muscles swing and tilt the arytenoids. Stretching the folds tighter raises the pitch; longer, thicker folds (as in most adult males) vibrate more slowly and sound lower.

check.q: What is the glottis?
check.a: The vocal folds together with the opening between them.

steps.title: The cat larynx
steps.text:
A cat larynx shows the same plan. Its thyroid cartilage is more wedge-shaped, and the epiglottis looks paler and more flexible than the hyaline cartilages around it because it is elastic cartilage. Cut in the midline, it shows the epiglottis, glottis, vestibular and vocal folds, and the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

As in us, the cat trachea lies ventral (in front of) the oesophagus.

check.q: In the cat, does the trachea lie ventral or dorsal to the oesophagus?
check.a: Ventral, as the trachea lies anterior to the oesophagus in humans.

practice.q: Which laryngeal cartilage is elastic cartilage?
practice.why: All the others, including the corniculate and cuneiform, are hyaline.

practice.q: Which are the true vocal cords?
practice.why: The vestibular folds above them are the false vocal cords.

practice.q: Which rises to seal the nasopharynx during swallowing?
practice.why: The epiglottis guards the larynx, not the nasopharynx.

practice.q: Put the pharynx in order from top to bottom
Why is the laryngeal prominence larger in males?
practice.a: Testosterone at puberty enlarges the thyroid cartilage (and lengthens the vocal folds).

practice.q: How do the intrinsic laryngeal muscles raise pitch?
practice.a: They move the arytenoid cartilages to tense (stretch) the vocal folds, which then vibrate faster.

practice.q: Name the small cartilages in the fold in front of the arytenoids, and the fat in front of the epiglottis.
practice.a: Cuneiform cartilages; pre-epiglottic adipose tissue.

practice.q: In the cat larynx, how does the thyroid cartilage differ from ours?
practice.why: Same cartilages, different shape.

title: Trachea and bronchial tree
summary: An open tube held by C-shaped rings, branching twenty-odd times down to the alveoli.
objectives: Describe the tracheal wall and why its cartilages are C-shaped
Follow the bronchial tree from the carina to the alveoli
Contrast bronchi with bronchioles
takeaways: C-shaped hyaline rings keep the trachea open; trachealis closes the back next to the oesophagus.
Respiratory epithelium + submucosa + hyaline cartilage + adventitia.
Main → lobar (one per lobe) → segmental (one per segment) → bronchioles.
Bronchioles have no cartilage and a muscular wall — the target in asthma.

steps.title: A tube that must not collapse
steps.text:
The trachea ('windpipe') runs from the cricoid cartilage to its split behind the sternal angle. It is held open by 16–20 C-shaped tracheal cartilages of hyaline cartilage.

The rings are open at the back. That gap is closed by the posterior tracheal membrane containing trachealis smooth muscle, which faces the oesophagus: a swallowed bolus can bulge forward into it, and trachealis narrows the lumen for a forceful cough.

check.q: Why are the tracheal cartilages open posteriorly?
check.a: So the oesophagus behind can expand during swallowing; trachealis spans the gap.

steps.title: The tracheal wall
steps.text:
From the lumen outward: respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells and basal stem cells) on a basement membrane; a lamina propria; a submucosa with seromucous glands; the hyaline cartilage ring; and an outer adventitia.

Goblet cells and glands make a mucus blanket, and the cilia beat it up toward the pharynx to be swallowed: the mucociliary escalator.

check.q: Which way do tracheal cilia move mucus?
check.a: Upward, toward the larynx and pharynx.

steps.title: Carina and the branching tree
steps.text:
At the bifurcation a keel-shaped ridge, the carina, divides the airway; its mucosa is exquisitely sensitive and triggers coughing. The trachea splits into the right and left main (primary) bronchi. The right is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects usually land there.

Each main bronchus gives lobar (secondary) bronchi, one per lobe (3 right, 2 left), and these give segmental (tertiary) bronchi, one per bronchopulmonary segment.
focus: Apical segmental bronchus of right lung (BI)

check.q: Why do inhaled foreign bodies usually enter the right main bronchus?
check.a: It is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

steps.title: From bronchi to bronchioles
steps.text:
Bronchi still have hyaline cartilage plates and respiratory epithelium. As the tubes shrink below about 1 mm they become bronchioles: no cartilage, and a wall made mostly of smooth muscle. That muscle is what constricts in asthma.

The last purely conducting tube is the terminal bronchiole. Then come respiratory bronchioles (with a few alveoli in their walls), alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and the alveoli themselves.

check.q: What two features separate a bronchiole from a bronchus?
check.a: No cartilage, and a wall dominated by smooth muscle.

practice.structure: Apical segmental bronchus of right lung (BI)

practice.q: Put the airways in order from largest to smallest
Which lies in the posterior tracheal membrane?
practice.why: The membranous part closes the open back of the C-rings.

practice.q: What is the carina?
practice.a: The keel-shaped ridge inside the tracheal bifurcation, where the main bronchi part; touching it triggers a strong cough.

practice.q: How many lobar bronchi are there on each side, and what does each segmental bronchus supply?
practice.a: Three on the right, two on the left; each segmental bronchus supplies one bronchopulmonary segment.

title: Lungs, pleurae and the cat lung
summary: Five human lobes, two layers of pleura coupled by a film of fluid, and two blood supplies.
objectives: Name the lobes of each lung and the cardiac notch
Explain how the pleurae couple the lung to the chest wall
Distinguish the pulmonary and bronchial blood supplies and the lymphatic drainage
Compare the lobes of the cat lung with the human lung
takeaways: Right lung: superior, middle, inferior. Left: superior, inferior, with a cardiac notch.
Parietal pleura lines the wall, visceral pleura covers the lung; fluid between them couples the two.
Pulmonary vessels carry blood for gas exchange; bronchial vessels feed the lung tissue.
Cat: 4 lobes on the right (including an accessory lobe), 3 on the left.

steps.title: Lobes and the cardiac notch
steps.text:
The right lung has three lobes, superior, middle and inferior, separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures. The left lung has only two, superior and inferior, because the heart takes up room: its anterior border is cut away as the cardiac notch.

The lungs sit in the pleural cavities on either side of the mediastinum, the central compartment holding the heart, great vessels, trachea and oesophagus.

check.q: Why does the left lung have only two lobes?
check.a: The heart lies to the left, leaving room for only a superior and an inferior lobe, with a cardiac notch.

steps.title: Two layers of pleura
steps.text:
The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall, diaphragm and mediastinum; the visceral pleura is fused to the lung surface. Between them the pleural cavity holds only a film of pleural fluid.

That fluid lubricates, and its surface tension holds the two layers together like wet glass slides. When the chest wall expands, the parietal pleura pulls the visceral pleura and the lung follows. Elastic fibres in the lung give it the recoil that empties it again.

check.q: What couples the lung to the chest wall?
check.a: The surface tension of the thin film of pleural fluid between parietal and visceral pleura.

steps.title: Two blood supplies and the lymph
steps.text:
Branches of the pulmonary arteries follow the bronchi and carry deoxygenated blood to the alveolar capillaries. Branches of the pulmonary veins run in the interlobular connective tissue and return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

The lung tissue itself is fed by small bronchial arteries and drained by bronchial veins, running with a bronchial nerve along the airways. Superficial (under the pleura) and deep lymphatic vessels drain to the pulmonary lymph nodes and on to the hilum.

check.q: Which vessels nourish the bronchial walls themselves?
check.a: The bronchial arteries (and veins).

steps.title: The cat lung
steps.text:
A cat has more lobes. Its right lung has four: superior, upper middle, lower middle (accessory) and inferior. The accessory lobe tucks behind the heart and has no human equivalent. Its left lung has three: superior, middle and inferior; the middle corresponds to our lingula.

Cut lung looks like fine sponge because the alveoli are microscopic. Below, the diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the liver.

check.q: How many lobes does each cat lung have?
check.a: Right 4 (superior, upper middle, lower middle/accessory, inferior); left 3 (superior, middle, inferior).

practice.q: Which layer of pleura covers the lung surface?
practice.why: Parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall and diaphragm.

practice.q: Which cat lung lobe has no human equivalent?
choices: Lower middle (accessory) lobe of the right lung
Superior lobe of the left lung
Inferior lobe of the right lung
Middle lobe of the left lung
practice.why: The cat's left middle lobe matches our lingula; the accessory lobe is extra.

practice.q: What occupies the mediastinum?
practice.a: The central compartment between the pleural cavities: heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus and more.

practice.q: What in a cat separates the thoracic cavity from the liver?
practice.a: The diaphragm.

practice.q: Where do pulmonary vein branches run, and which lymphatic vessels drain the lung?
practice.a: In the interlobular connective tissue; superficial (subpleural) and deep lymphatic vessels drain to the pulmonary nodes.

title: Alveoli and the respiratory membrane
summary: Where gas exchange happens, the cells that make it possible, and what disease does to them.
objectives: Name the parts of the respiratory zone and recognise them on a lung section
Describe type I and type II pneumocytes and alveolar macrophages
List the layers of the respiratory membrane
Relate emphysema, asthma, fibrosis and smoker's lung to structure
takeaways: Type I cells (simple squamous) form the exchange surface; type II cells make surfactant.
Respiratory membrane = alveolar epithelium + fused basement membrane + capillary endothelium.
Emphysema destroys alveolar walls (obstructive); fibrosis and TB stiffen the lung (restrictive).
Wheezes come from narrowed airways; crackles (rattles) from fluid or secretions.

steps.title: The respiratory zone
steps.text:
Past the terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchioles have alveoli budding from their walls. They lead into alveolar ducts, then clusters called alveolar sacs, each a ring of alveoli.

Neighbouring alveoli share thin interalveolar walls carrying dense pulmonary capillaries and elastic fibres. On a lung section you see lace-like alveoli, a bronchiole with folded epithelium, alveolar ducts and sacs, and blood vessels with red blood cells.

check.q: What distinguishes a respiratory bronchiole from a terminal bronchiole?
check.a: Alveoli open from its wall, so some gas exchange happens there.

steps.title: The cells of the alveolus
steps.text:
Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin simple squamous epithelium covering about 90% of the alveolar surface; gas crosses them. Type II pneumocytes (septal cells) are rounder and secrete surfactant, which lowers the surface tension of the fluid lining so alveoli do not collapse.

Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) wander the air spaces eating particles and microbes.

check.q: What does surfactant do, and which cell makes it?
check.a: It lowers surface tension in the alveoli; type II pneumocytes (septal cells) make it.

steps.title: The respiratory membrane
steps.text:
Oxygen and carbon dioxide move by diffusion across the respiratory membrane: the type I alveolar epithelium, a fused basement membrane and the pulmonary capillary endothelium. Together they are about half a micrometre thick.

With roughly 70 m² of alveolar surface and red blood cells squeezing through the capillaries in single file, gas exchange is complete in a fraction of a second.

check.q: Name the three layers of the respiratory membrane.
check.a: Alveolar (type I) epithelium, fused basement membrane, capillary endothelium.

steps.title: When alveoli fail
steps.text:
Smoker's lung is streaked with dark particles held in macrophages and has destroyed alveoli. In emphysema alveolar walls break down: less surface area, poorer O2 diffusion and air trapping — an obstructive disorder that raises residual volume. In asthma the bronchioles constrict, raising airway resistance (also obstructive).

Tuberculosis and pulmonary fibrosis scar the lung and reduce its elasticity and compliance: restrictive disorders that shrink the capacities. Wheezing suggests narrowed airways; rattling (crackles) suggests fluid or mucus.

check.q: Is emphysema obstructive or restrictive, and why?
check.a: Obstructive: lost alveolar walls remove the elastic pull that holds small airways open, so air is trapped and residual volume rises.

practice.q: Which cells cover most of the alveolar surface?
practice.why: Simple squamous type I cells make the thin exchange surface.

practice.q: Which disorder is restrictive?
practice.why: Fibrosis and TB stiffen the lung, lowering compliance and capacities.

practice.q: Put the respiratory zone in order
Besides alveoli, what can you pick out on a lung section?
practice.a: A bronchiole with folded epithelium, alveolar ducts and sacs, and blood vessels full of red blood cells; elastic fibers sit in the interalveolar walls.

practice.q: What is a dust cell?
practice.a: An alveolar macrophage that engulfs particles in the air spaces.

practice.q: What does a smoker's lung look like?
practice.a: Dark particulate deposits (in macrophages) throughout, with destroyed alveoli.

practice.q: What do wheezes and rattles (crackles) suggest?
practice.a: Wheezes: narrowed airways. Rattles/crackles: fluid or mucus congesting the airways.

practice.q: Why is gas exchange so fast?
choices: A huge surface area and a very thin respiratory membrane
Active transport of O2 by type I cells
practice.why: Diffusion rate rises with area and falls with thickness.

title: Pressure, volume and a breath
summary: Boyle's law in the chest: how the diaphragm drives air in and recoil lets it out.
objectives: State Boyle's law and apply it to inspiration and expiration
Give the pressures at rest, during inspiration and during expiration
Map the parts of a bell jar model onto the body
Calculate minute ventilation
takeaways: Air moves from high to low pressure; volume up = pressure down (Boyle's law).
Atmosphere 760 mmHg; alveoli ~759 in inspiration, ~761 in expiration, 760 at rest.
Quiet inspiration is active (diaphragm); quiet expiration is passive recoil.
Minute ventilation = rate × tidal volume, e.g. 12 × 500 mL = 6 L/min.

steps.title: Boyle's law runs the chest
steps.text:
Pulmonary ventilation is simply air moving down a pressure gradient. Boyle's law: at a constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume — enlarge the container and the pressure falls.

Atmospheric (barometric) pressure at sea level is 760 mmHg. At the end of a quiet expiration the intraalveolar pressure is also 760 mmHg, so no air flows.

check.q: State Boyle's law.
check.a: At constant temperature, gas pressure is inversely proportional to volume.

steps.title: Inspiration
steps.text:
In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostals lift the ribs. The thoracic cavity enlarges, the pleurae drag the lungs outward, and intraalveolar pressure falls to about 759 mmHg.

Air now flows in from the 760 mmHg atmosphere until the pressures are equal again. Even quiet inspiration is active: it needs muscle contraction.

check.q: What is the intraalveolar pressure during inspiration, roughly?
check.a: About 759 mmHg, 1 mmHg below atmospheric.

steps.title: Expiration
steps.text:
In quiet expiration the diaphragm relaxes and domes upward, and the elastic lung and chest wall recoil. Thoracic volume falls, intraalveolar pressure rises to about 761 mmHg, and air flows out.

Quiet expiration is passive. Forced expiration adds the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles to squeeze the chest further.

check.q: Why is quiet expiration called passive?
check.a: It needs no muscle contraction: the diaphragm relaxes and elastic recoil does the work.

steps.title: The bell jar model
steps.text:
A bell jar model makes the mechanics visible. The jar is the thoracic cage, the balloons are the lungs, the rubber sheet across the bottom is the diaphragm, and the Y-tube through the stopper is the airway (nose, trachea and bronchi).

Pull the sheet down and the jar's volume rises, pressure inside falls and the balloons inflate; let it go and they deflate.

check.q: In the bell jar model, what does the rubber sheet represent?
check.a: The diaphragm.

steps.title: Breathing rate and minute ventilation
steps.text:
A relaxed adult takes about 12–15 breaths per minute. Minute ventilation (minute volume) is breathing rate × tidal volume: 12 × 500 mL = 6 L/min.

During exercise the ventilation rate climbs, and so does the depth of each breath. The main driver is the rising carbon dioxide in the blood, together with the muscles' demand for oxygen.

check.q: A person breathes 15 times a minute with a tidal volume of 400 mL. What is the minute ventilation?

practice.q: During inspiration, intraalveolar pressure is about:
practice.why: Enlarging the thorax drops alveolar pressure below the 760 mmHg atmosphere.

practice.q: What happens to lung volume and pressure when the diaphragm contracts?
practice.why: Boyle's law: pressure is inversely related to volume.

practice.q: Put inspiration in order
Map the bell jar model: jar, balloons, rubber sheet, tube/stopper.
practice.a: Jar = thoracic cage; balloons = lungs; rubber sheet = diaphragm; tube through stopper = airway (nose, trachea, bronchi).

practice.q: What is atmospheric (barometric) pressure at sea level?
practice.a: 760 mmHg.

practice.q: Why does ventilation rate rise with exercise?
choices: Rising blood CO2 and O2 demand
practice.why: Chemoreceptors respond mainly to CO2 (and H+).

practice.q: What is the intraalveolar pressure at the end of a quiet expiration?
practice.a: 760 mmHg, equal to atmospheric, so no air flows.

title: Lung volumes and capacities
summary: Four volumes, four capacities, and what a spirogram does and does not show.
objectives: Read tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual volume off a spirogram
Build the four capacities from the volumes
Explain predicted and percent-predicted vital capacity
Predict how obstructive and restrictive disease change the numbers
takeaways: TV 500, IRV 3000, ERV 1100, RV 1200 mL (typical adult).
IC = TV + IRV; FRC = ERV + RV; VC = IRV + TV + ERV; TLC = VC + RV.
Residual volume (and so FRC and TLC) cannot be measured with a spirometer.
≥80% of predicted VC is normal; obstruction raises RV, restriction lowers capacities.

steps.title: Spirometers and the spirogram
steps.text:
A spirometer measures the air moved in and out. A handheld spirometer (a vane turned by the breath) measures exhaled air only; a wet spirometer uses a floating bell over water; an airflow transducer measures flow and integrates it to volume.

The trace of volume against time is a spirogram. Quiet breaths make small waves; maximal breaths show the reserves above and below them.

check.q: What does a spirogram plot?
check.a: Lung volume against time.

steps.title: The four volumes
steps.text:
Tidal volume (TV), about 500 mL, is a normal quiet breath. Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV), about 3000 mL, is the extra you can force in after a normal inhalation. Expiratory reserve volume (ERV), about 1100 mL (1000–1200), is the extra you can force out after a normal exhalation.

Residual volume (RV), about 1200 mL, stays in the lungs after a maximal exhalation. It never leaves, so a spirometer cannot measure it.

check.q: Which lung volume can a spirometer not measure, and why?
check.a: Residual volume: it never leaves the lungs, so it never passes through the spirometer.

steps.title: Capacities are sums
steps.text:
A capacity is the sum of two or more volumes.

Inspiratory capacity IC = TV + IRV (~3500 mL). Functional residual capacity FRC = ERV + RV (~2300 mL), the air left after a quiet breath out. Vital capacity VC = IRV + TV + ERV (~4600 mL; 4500–5500 in young adults). Total lung capacity TLC = VC + RV (~6000 mL).

Rearranged, IRV = VC − (ERV + TV), which is how IRV is often worked out.

check.q: VC is 4800 mL, ERV 1200 mL and TV 500 mL. What is IRV?

steps.title: Predicted values and disease
steps.text:
Vital capacity depends on sex, height and age: it is larger in taller people and in males, and falls with age. A predicted vital capacity is read from tables using those three.

Percent of predicted = measured ÷ predicted × 100; 80% or more is normal. Obstructive disorders such as asthma and emphysema trap air and raise residual volume; restrictive disorders such as fibrosis reduce vital and total capacities.

check.q: Measured VC is 3600 mL and predicted is 4800 mL. Is this normal?
check.a: 3600 ÷ 4800 = 75% of predicted, below the 80% cut-off, so it is reduced.

practice.q: A normal quiet breath is the:
practice.why: TV is about 500 mL at rest.

practice.q: Functional residual capacity equals:
practice.why: FRC is what remains after a quiet expiration.

practice.q: Total lung capacity equals:
practice.why: About 6000 mL in a young adult.

practice.q: Give typical values for TV, IRV, ERV and RV.
Define inspiratory capacity and give its formula.
practice.a: The most you can inhale from the end of a quiet expiration: IC = TV + IRV.

practice.q: Write vital capacity as a sum of volumes.
practice.a: VC = IRV + TV + ERV (about 4500–5500 mL).

practice.q: Which instrument measures exhaled air only?
practice.why: You can only blow into a handheld spirometer.

practice.q: How does emphysema change residual volume?
practice.why: Obstructive disease traps air behind collapsing small airways.

practice.q: What is a normal percent of predicted vital capacity?
practice.a: 80% or more.

practice.q: Name three things that determine predicted vital capacity.
practice.a: Sex, height and age (larger in males and taller people, smaller with age).

practice.q: Put these in order from smallest to largest

title: Airflow, resistance and the flow–volume loop
summary: Why airway radius rules resistance, and how one loop tells obstructive from restrictive disease.
objectives: Relate airflow to pressure gradient and resistance
Explain why airway radius dominates resistance
Read a normal flow–volume loop and recognise obstructive and restrictive shapes
takeaways: Flow = ΔP ÷ R; halving the radius raises resistance about sixteen-fold.
Flow–volume loop: expiration above the line with a sharp peak, inspiration a rounded curve below.
Obstructive: scooped expiratory limb at high lung volumes. Restrictive: a small, narrow loop.

steps.title: Flow, pressure and resistance
steps.text:
Airflow is proportional to the pressure gradient and inversely proportional to airway resistance: F = ΔP ÷ R. The biggest control on resistance is the airway radius; resistance rises with the fourth power of narrowing, so a small squeeze matters a lot.

Breathing through one nostril, or bronchoconstriction in asthma, narrows the path, raises resistance and slows flow for the same effort.

check.q: What single factor most determines airway resistance?
check.a: The radius of the airway.

steps.title: Reading a flow–volume loop
steps.text:
A flow–volume loop plots airflow (vertical) against lung volume (horizontal) during a maximal breath out and in. Expiration is drawn above the baseline as positive flow, inspiration below as negative; the volume axis runs from total lung capacity to residual volume.

Normal expiration shoots up to a sharp peak expiratory flow, then declines almost linearly to the baseline. Inspiration is a rounded curve beneath.

check.q: Where does the expiratory limb of a normal loop reach its highest flow?
check.a: Early, just after starting from total lung capacity: the peak expiratory flow.

steps.title: Loops in disease
steps.text:
In obstructive disease (asthma, emphysema) the peak is lower and the expiratory limb is scooped out (concave) as small airways close; the loop sits at high lung volumes because air is trapped.

In restrictive disease (fibrosis) the loop keeps a near-normal shape but is small and narrow, shifted toward low volumes. Pulmonary function tests like this are how lung disease is classified.

check.q: Which disease pattern gives a scooped (concave) expiratory limb?
check.a: Obstructive disease.

practice.q: If airway radius halves, resistance:
practice.why: Resistance varies with 1/r⁴.

practice.q: In a flow–volume loop, expiration is drawn:
practice.why: Inspiration forms the rounded curve below.

practice.q: A small, narrow loop of normal shape suggests:
practice.why: Restriction lowers the volumes but not the flow pattern.

practice.q: Write the relationship between airflow, pressure gradient and resistance.
practice.a: Flow = ΔP ÷ R.

practice.q: Why does breathing through one nostril feel harder?
practice.a: The narrower path raises airway resistance, so flow falls for the same pressure difference.

practice.q: Between which two volumes does the flow–volume loop run?
practice.a: From total lung capacity to residual volume.

practice.q: What is the peak expiratory flow?
practice.a: The highest flow reached, just after a forced expiration begins.

title: Breath sounds, CO2 and CPR
summary: Where to listen, how breathing sets blood pH, and the numbers of chest compressions.
objectives: Describe where tracheal, bronchial and vesicular sounds are heard
Name the borders of the triangle of auscultation
Write the carbonic acid equation and relate ventilation to pH
State the compression site, rate and ratio in CPR
takeaways: Triangle of auscultation: trapezius, latissimus dorsi, medial border of scapula.
CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−; most CO2 travels as bicarbonate.
Hypoventilation → acidosis; hyperventilation → alkalosis. One pH unit = tenfold H+.
CPR: body of sternum, 100–120 per minute, 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

steps.title: Listening to the chest
steps.text:
Auscultation means listening with a stethoscope. Tracheal and bronchial sounds are loud and harsh, heard over the trachea just below the larynx. Over the lung fields you hear soft, smooth vesicular sounds as air fills the alveoli.

Abnormal sounds suggest disease: wheezes (whistling) from narrowed airways, crackles or rattles from fluid or mucus in the airways.

check.q: Where are tracheal and bronchial sounds best heard?
check.a: Over the trachea just inferior to the larynx.

steps.title: The triangle of auscultation
steps.text:
On the back, one spot has little muscle between skin and ribs: the triangle of auscultation. Its borders are the trapezius (medially), the latissimus dorsi (below) and the medial border of the scapula, near its inferior angle.

Breath sounds come through more clearly here. Asking the patient to fold the arms and lean forward pulls the scapulae apart and enlarges the triangle.

check.q: Name the three borders of the triangle of auscultation.
check.a: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula.

steps.title: Carbon dioxide makes acid
steps.text:
Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which splits into a hydrogen ion and a bicarbonate ion: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−. Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells speeds the first step, and most CO2 travels in blood as bicarbonate.

Breathe out through a straw into water containing a litmus indicator and it turns red: exhaled breath makes the water acid.

check.q: In what form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
check.a: As bicarbonate ions.

steps.title: Breathing sets the pH
steps.text:
The pH scale is logarithmic: one unit is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion. Blood is kept slightly alkaline, pH 7.35–7.45.

Breathing too little lets CO2 build up, pushing the equation right: more H+, lower pH (respiratory acidosis). Hyperventilation blows CO2 off, pulls the equation left and raises the pH (alkalosis). During exercise CO2 output rises and ventilation climbs to match it.

check.q: What does hyperventilation do to blood pH, and why?
check.a: Raises it: CO2 is blown off, so less carbonic acid and fewer hydrogen ions form.

steps.title: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation
steps.text:
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) keeps blood moving to the brain when the heart stops, for example after a myocardial infarction, drug overdose, drowning, trauma or a blocked airway.

Chest compressions go on the lower half of the body of the sternum, 100–120 per minute and about 5 cm deep. Trained rescuers give 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths; an untrained bystander should give hands-only CPR.

check.q: What compression-to-breath ratio do trained rescuers use?
check.a: 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

practice.q: What happens to blood pH if CO2 accumulates?
practice.why: More CO2 means more carbonic acid and more H+.

practice.q: A pH change from 7.4 to 6.4 means hydrogen ions have:
practice.why: The pH scale is logarithmic.

practice.q: Put the CO2 reaction in order
Chest compressions in adult CPR are given at:
practice.why: Push hard and fast on the body of the sternum.

practice.q: Name situations where CPR may be needed.
practice.a: Cardiac arrest (e.g. myocardial infarction), drug overdose, drowning, trauma, airway obstruction.

practice.q: What colour does a litmus indicator turn when exhaled breath is bubbled through it, and why?
practice.a: Red: CO2 forms carbonic acid, making the water acidic.

practice.q: Contrast tracheal/bronchial sounds with vesicular sounds.
practice.a: Tracheal and bronchial: loud, harsh, over the trachea. Vesicular: soft and smooth over the lung fields.

practice.q: What should an untrained bystander do?
practice.a: Hands-only CPR: continuous chest compressions.
